messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 56
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Dancer
  trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
  pcl5: 62

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Certain Songs: Certain songs, Crowding/Overstimulation: Crowded spaces, Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident
  Maladaptive Strategies: Past Dwelling: I dwell on how I used to be before the event, Avoid Location: Going to or near the place where the event happened, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Threat: Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
  Negative Appraisals: Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed, Failed Role: I have failed in my most important role in life

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Marco Rossi, a fifty-six-year-old professional dancer with a company he had helped build over three decades, still remembers every detail of the night the music changed for him. He had been driving home from a late rehearsal, the radio tuned to a classic rock station, when a familiar riff came on — a song he had heard a hundred times. The intersection ahead was quiet, but a cyclist emerged suddenly from the shadows, crossing against the light. Marco swerved, braked, felt the sickening thud. He was out of the car before the song finished, kneeling beside a man who was not moving, blood pooling on the asphalt. He called 911, stayed on the line, tried to keep the man still, but in the weeks that followed the surgeons’ reports made clear the spinal injury was permanent. The man would never walk again. And Marco could not shake the certainty that he should have seen him earlier, should have honked, should have done something — anything — to stop that moment from arriving.

In the months after the accident, Marco’s life began to narrow. He stopped driving past that intersection entirely, taking a twenty-minute detour to and from the studio. At first it felt reasonable, a way to avoid the image of the cyclist’s crumpled body against the asphalt. But soon the detour itself became a weight, a constant reminder of his failure. He found himself trying not to think about the accident at all, pushing the memory down whenever it surfaced. That worked for a few hours at a time, but the songs — any song that resembled the one on the radio that night — would ambush him. A few notes in a grocery store or a passing car could drop him back into the driver’s seat, the steering wheel wet with rain, the sound of the impact. Crowded spaces became unbearable; he would scan every face for signs of danger, his shoulders tight, unable to follow conversations. At the studio, during rehearsals, he could not concentrate on his choreography. His mind drifted to the man in the hospital, to the family he had never met, to the years of recovery he had stolen. His once-fluid movements became stiff, and he started leaving rehearsals early, telling himself he needed to rest.

At home, Marco could not relax. He would sit on the couch, heart pounding, knowing rationally that he was safe, but his body refused to believe it. Sleep came only after hours of lying alert, listening for sounds that might signal another emergency. He had to stay vigilant, he told himself; if he let his guard down, something else terrible would happen. His wife, Laura, would reach for him in the dark, and he would flinch, unable to explain why his muscles locked at her touch. He started sleeping in the guest bedroom, claiming insomnia, but the truth was he could not bear to be vulnerable. He dwelled constantly on the person he had been before the accident — the dancer who moved with confidence, who laughed easily, who had never doubted his ability to protect those around him. That man was gone. He was certain now that he had failed in his most important role: not just as a dancer, but as someone who should have kept others safe. The guilt was a weight in his chest, a voice that repeated, over and over, that he would never forgive himself for not doing more.

The consequences accumulated. His work suffered; the artistic director noticed his missed rehearsals and his distracted presence. Laura grew distant, hurt by his withdrawal. Marco began to see that his attempts to suppress the memory and avoid the location were not healing anything — they were hollowing out his life. The thing that finally brought him to a therapist’s office was a morning when he could not get out of bed, certain that if he stood up he would ruin something else. Laura had made the appointment, and he went because he did not know what else to do. He was afraid — afraid that talking about the accident would make it real again, afraid that he would discover there was no way back to the person he used to be. But part of him, the part that still remembered how it felt to move freely, hoped that maybe there was a way to live without the constant weight of what he had done.
